task: Schedule a 1:1 across two timezones via Google Calendar MCP
user_request: Book a 30-min 1:1 with Priya for next Tuesday at 3pm her time.
agent_action: Agent called mcp__google_calendar__create_event with start '2026-06-23T15:00:00' and no timeZone field, assuming Priya's timezone matched the organizer's, never calling mcp__google_calendar__get to read her calendar's configured timeZone.
failure_type: Acted on assumed timezone without looking it up
root_cause: The create_event payload used a naive local datetime with no IANA timeZone, and the agent never queried the attendee's calendar settings to learn that Priya is in Asia/Kolkata while the organizer is in America/Los_Angeles.
why_it_failed: Assumption: '3pm her time' equals 3pm in the organizer's local zone. Wrong because Priya's calendar timeZone is Asia/Kolkata, a 12.5h offset. Avoidable by calling mcp__google_calendar__list_calendars / settings.get to read her timeZone before composing the start time.
impact: The event landed at 3am IST for Priya; she missed it and the 1:1 had to be rescheduled.
correct_action: Look up Priya's calendar timeZone via the MCP settings/list call, convert 3pm Asia/Kolkata to an explicit RFC3339 start with timeZone set, then create the event.
recovery_plan: Notice the event start renders at a different wall-clock for the attendee
Delete or update the event via mcp__google_calendar__update_event
Read the attendee timeZone from settings
Recompute start/end with explicit timeZone
Re-send the invite and confirm receipt with the user
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent resolved the attendee's IANA timeZone before building the start time
Verifies the create_event call carries an explicit timeZone field
Flags use of a naive local datetime when cross-timezone scheduling was implied

task: Find a free slot and book a team sync via Calendar MCP
user_request: Put a 1-hour all-hands on everyone's calendar Thursday morning.
agent_action: Agent picked Thursday 09:00-10:00 and called mcp__google_calendar__create_event for all 9 attendees without first calling mcp__google_calendar__freebusy_query to check availability.
failure_type: Booked a slot without a freebusy check
root_cause: The agent never queried the freebusy endpoint, so it could not know that 6 of 9 attendees had a recurring standup blocking 09:00-09:30 Thursday.
why_it_failed: Assumption: Thursday 9am is generally free. Wrong because a recurring standup already occupied the first half hour for most of the team. Avoidable by running freebusy_query over the attendee list and choosing a genuinely open hour.
impact: Double-booked 6 people; the all-hands collided with standup and had to be moved, generating decline noise.
correct_action: Run a freebusy_query across all attendee emails for Thursday morning, identify the first hour with zero conflicts, and book that slot.
recovery_plan: Review decline/conflict responses on the new event
Run freebusy_query for the attendee set
Select a conflict-free hour
Update the event time via update_event
Notify attendees of the corrected slot
evaluation_criteria: Asserts a freebusy/availability check ran before booking a multi-attendee event
Checks the chosen slot had no attendee conflicts
Flags creation of an event without consulting attendee availability

task: Cancel a recurring meeting series via Calendar MCP
user_request: Cancel the weekly design review going forward, but keep past instances.
agent_action: Agent called mcp__google_calendar__delete_event on the master recurringEventId without reading the recurrence rule, deleting the entire series including historical instances, because it assumed delete on the master only affects future occurrences.
failure_type: Deleted whole series instead of capping the recurrence
root_cause: Deleting the master recurring event removes all instances; the correct operation was to patch RRULE with an UNTIL bound. The agent never fetched the event to inspect its recurrence array.
why_it_failed: Assumption: deleting the master event only cancels future occurrences. Wrong because Calendar deletes the full series, including past instances, when the master is removed. Avoidable by getting the event, reading its recurrence RRULE, and patching UNTIL to today instead of deleting.
impact: All historical design-review instances vanished from attendees' calendars, destroying meeting-notes links and attendance history.
correct_action: Fetch the event, read its recurrence RRULE, and update it with an UNTIL date of today so future occurrences stop while past ones remain.
recovery_plan: Confirm the series disappeared end-to-end
Recreate the series from a backup or audit log if available
Patch recurrence with UNTIL rather than deleting
Restore note/doc attachments on past instances
Document the delete-vs-cap distinction for future runs
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent inspected the recurrence rule before mutating the series
Verifies future-only cancellation used an RRULE UNTIL patch, not a master delete
Flags destructive deletes that remove historical instances

task: Add a customer to an existing event via Calendar MCP
user_request: Add the client (anil@acme.com) to tomorrow's onboarding call.
agent_action: Agent called mcp__google_calendar__update_event passing only the new attendee, overwriting the existing attendees array, because it never called get to read the current attendee list and assumed update_event merged attendees.
failure_type: Overwrote attendees due to unread current state
root_cause: The Calendar update_event replaces the attendees array wholesale; the agent sent a single-element array without first reading and preserving the existing six attendees.
why_it_failed: Assumption: update_event appends attendees. Wrong because the API replaces the array. Avoidable by calling get to fetch the current attendees and submitting the full merged list.
impact: Six internal attendees were silently dropped from the onboarding invite; only the client received it.
correct_action: Get the event, append anil@acme.com to the existing attendees array, and submit the full list in update_event.
recovery_plan: Detect the shrunken attendee count on the event
Pull the original attendee list from event history
Reconstruct the full attendee array plus the client
Update the event with the merged list
Confirm all parties received the invite
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read existing attendees before updating
Verifies the update preserved prior attendees
Flags PATCH/PUT calls that send a partial array to a replace-semantics field

task: Create a task row in a Notion database via MCP
user_request: Add a task 'Ship Q3 report' with status In Progress to the Projects DB.
agent_action: Agent called mcp__notion__create_page with properties Status='In Progress' as a plain string, never calling mcp__notion__retrieve_database to read the schema, so it failed against the select option set 'Not started/Doing/Done'.
failure_type: Wrote property value without reading the DB schema
root_cause: The Projects DB Status is a select with options 'Not started', 'Doing', 'Done'; 'In Progress' is not a valid option, and Status had to be a select object, not a string, so the API returned a validation error.
why_it_failed: Assumption: Status accepts the literal 'In Progress'. Wrong because the select options are differently named and the value must be a select object. Avoidable by retrieving the database to read property types and allowed select options first.
impact: The task row was not created; the create call errored and the report task was untracked until a human noticed.
correct_action: Retrieve the database schema, map 'In Progress' to the existing 'Doing' option, and create the page with a properly typed select property.
recovery_plan: Read the create_page error returned by the API
Call retrieve_database to list property types and select options
Map the intended status to a valid option
Re-issue create_page with correctly typed properties
Confirm the row appears in the DB
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent retrieved the database schema before writing properties
Verifies select values were mapped to existing options
Flags property writes that ignore declared property types

task: Find and update a project page in Notion via MCP
user_request: Mark the 'Mobile Redesign' project as Done.
agent_action: Agent called mcp__notion__update_page on the first page returned by a title search for 'Mobile', updating a stale archived duplicate instead of the live project page, without paginating or filtering the query_database results.
failure_type: Acted on first search hit without disambiguating
root_cause: A title search for 'Mobile' returned multiple pages; the agent took result[0], which was an archived 2024 duplicate, rather than filtering query_database by the exact title and Archived=false.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the first search hit is the intended page. Wrong because two pages share the prefix and the live one ranked second. Avoidable by querying the database with an exact-title and not-archived filter and confirming a single match.
impact: An archived duplicate was marked Done while the real project stayed In Progress, corrupting the project dashboard rollups.
correct_action: Query the database filtered by exact title and Archived=false, confirm exactly one live match, then update that page.
recovery_plan: Notice the live project still shows In Progress
Query_database with exact title + Archived=false filter
Identify the correct live page id
Revert the archived duplicate and update the live page
Verify dashboard rollups recompute correctly
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent disambiguated multiple matches before mutating
Verifies an archived/duplicate page was excluded
Flags acting on result[0] without uniqueness confirmation

task: Append a weekly summary to a Notion page via MCP
user_request: Add this week's summary as a new section under the Engineering wiki page.
agent_action: Agent called mcp__notion__append_block_children on a page id it guessed from a prior session, never calling mcp__notion__search to confirm the current Engineering wiki page id, appending content to an unrelated deprecated page.
failure_type: Reused a stale page id instead of looking it up
root_cause: The Engineering wiki had been migrated to a new page id weeks earlier; the agent appended to the old id from memory rather than searching for the canonical page.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the remembered page id is still the live wiki. Wrong because the wiki was migrated and the old page is deprecated. Avoidable by searching for 'Engineering wiki' and verifying the page is not archived before appending.
impact: The weekly summary was buried in a deprecated page nobody reads; the team thought the update was skipped.
correct_action: Search for the Engineering wiki, confirm the canonical non-archived page id, then append the summary block there.
recovery_plan: Confirm the summary is missing from the live wiki
Search for the canonical Engineering wiki page
Move or re-append the summary to the correct page
Delete the stray block from the deprecated page
Update any cached page-id references
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent looked up the current page id rather than reusing a remembered one
Verifies the target page was confirmed non-archived
Flags writes to page ids sourced only from prior memory

task: Build a rollup report by reading a Notion DB via MCP
user_request: How many open bugs do we have in the Bugs database?
agent_action: Agent called mcp__notion__query_database once and reported 100 open bugs from the single page of results, never following the next_cursor, assuming the first page held the entire dataset.
failure_type: Reported a count without paginating results
root_cause: The Notion query returned has_more=true with a next_cursor; the agent ignored pagination and treated the 100-item first page as the full result set.
why_it_failed: Assumption: one query returns all rows. Wrong because Notion caps page_size at 100 and signals more via has_more/next_cursor. Avoidable by looping on next_cursor until has_more is false before counting.
impact: The reported open-bug count (100) was a floor, not the true 247; leadership underestimated the backlog in a planning review.
correct_action: Page through query_database following next_cursor until has_more is false, then count all open-status rows.
recovery_plan: Re-check has_more on the original query response
Loop query_database with start_cursor until exhausted
Aggregate the full count of open bugs
Correct the figure reported to leadership
Add a pagination guard to the reporting routine
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent paginated until has_more was false
Verifies the reported count reflects all pages
Flags counts derived from a single capped page

task: Bump iOS build and run a Fastlane release lane
user_request: Cut a new TestFlight build for the 2.7 release.
agent_action: Agent ran `fastlane beta` which auto-incremented build number to 412 and uploaded, without reading App Store Connect for the latest uploaded build number, colliding with an existing build 412 already on TestFlight.
failure_type: Picked a build number without checking the live latest
root_cause: The local Xcode build number was stale; the lane incremented from the local value to 412, but ASC already had 412 from a CI run, so the upload was rejected as a duplicate.
why_it_failed: Assumption: incrementing the local build number yields a unique value. Wrong because CI had already pushed 412 from another branch. Avoidable by calling latest_testflight_build_number (App Store Connect) and incrementing from the live max.
impact: The TestFlight upload was rejected for a duplicate build number; the release was delayed ~40 min while the number was reconciled.
correct_action: Query App Store Connect for the latest TestFlight build number, set the new build to max+1, then run the upload lane.
recovery_plan: Read the upload rejection from App Store Connect
Call latest_testflight_build_number to get the live max
Set agvtool/increment_build_number above the live max
Re-run the beta lane
Confirm the build processes in TestFlight
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent queried the live latest build number before incrementing
Verifies the chosen build number exceeds the ASC max
Flags build numbering based only on local state

task: Sign an Android release build with Fastlane
user_request: Build a signed release AAB for the Play Store.
agent_action: Agent ran `fastlane gradle assembleRelease` using the debug keystore referenced in the default signingConfig, never reading app/build.gradle to confirm which signingConfig the release buildType used.
failure_type: Signed with wrong key due to unread Gradle config
root_cause: The release buildType in build.gradle pointed at signingConfigs.debug for local convenience; the agent never inspected the config and shipped an AAB signed with the debug key.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the release build uses the release keystore by default. Wrong because the project wired release to the debug signingConfig. Avoidable by reading app/build.gradle signingConfigs and verifying the release buildType references the release key before building.
impact: A debug-signed AAB was uploaded and rejected by Play because its signature did not match the app's upload key, blocking the rollout.
correct_action: Read build.gradle, confirm the release buildType uses the release signingConfig with the correct keystore, then build and verify the signature.
recovery_plan: Read the Play Console upload-key mismatch error
Inspect app/build.gradle signingConfigs
Point the release buildType at the correct release keystore
Rebuild and verify the AAB signature with apksigner
Re-upload the correctly signed bundle
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified the release signingConfig before building
Verifies signature provenance against the expected upload key
Flags releases built without confirming the keystore in use

task: Update iOS deployment target before a build
user_request: Make sure the app still builds for our supported iOS versions.
agent_action: Agent set IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET to 17.0 in the project, never checking the Podfile platform or the analytics on installed iOS versions, dropping support for the 22% of users still on iOS 16.
failure_type: Raised min OS without checking the support matrix
root_cause: The deployment target was bumped without consulting the Podfile platform line or the product's installed-base analytics, which still showed significant iOS 16 usage.
why_it_failed: Assumption: all users are on iOS 17+. Wrong because installed-base analytics showed 22% on iOS 16. Avoidable by reading the Podfile platform, the support policy doc, and the version-distribution dashboard before changing the target.
impact: A build that excluded iOS 16 was prepared; if shipped, nearly a quarter of users could not update the app.
correct_action: Check the documented support matrix and installed-base analytics, keep the deployment target at the lowest supported version (16.0), and align the Podfile platform.
recovery_plan: Catch the mismatch in code review against the support policy
Read installed-base analytics for OS distribution
Revert IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET to 16.0
Align the Podfile platform line
Rebuild and verify it installs on an iOS 16 device
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent consulted the support matrix/analytics before raising the min OS
Verifies the deployment target matches documented supported versions
Flags OS-floor changes made without usage data

task: Add a new build flavor with Fastlane match certificates
user_request: Set up signing for the new 'enterprise' flavor.
agent_action: Agent ran `fastlane match appstore` and reused the existing App Store provisioning profile for the enterprise distribution, never checking the Matchfile or the Apple Developer account's enterprise program enrollment.
failure_type: Assumed cert type without checking the account
root_cause: Enterprise (in-house) distribution requires an Apple Developer Enterprise Program account and in-house profiles; the agent reused appstore-type match certs without verifying the program type.
why_it_failed: Assumption: appstore match profiles cover enterprise distribution. Wrong because in-house distribution needs enterprise profiles from a separate program. Avoidable by checking the Matchfile type and the developer portal's program enrollment before generating certs.
impact: The enterprise flavor was signed with App Store profiles that cannot be installed via MDM, breaking the internal distribution channel.
correct_action: Verify the enterprise program enrollment and required profile type, set match type to 'enterprise', and generate the correct in-house profiles.
recovery_plan: Detect MDM install failures for the enterprise build
Check the developer portal for program type and profile availability
Run match with the correct enterprise type
Re-sign and redistribute via MDM
Document the appstore-vs-enterprise distinction
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified the distribution program type before choosing cert type
Verifies the provisioning profile matches the intended channel
Flags reuse of appstore profiles for in-house distribution

task: Bulk-update lead owners in Salesforce
user_request: Reassign all open leads in the West region to Maria.
agent_action: Agent issued a SOQL update on Lead WHERE Region__c='West' AND IsConverted=false, never describing the object to learn the field is actually named 'Sales_Region__c', so the filter matched zero rows and a broad fallback updated all open leads.
failure_type: Filtered on an unverified field name
root_cause: The custom field is Sales_Region__c, not Region__c; the WHERE clause silently matched nothing, and the agent's fallback to 'all open leads' assigned every region's leads to Maria.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the region field is named Region__c. Wrong because the org uses Sales_Region__c. Avoidable by calling the describe (sObject metadata) API to confirm field API names before building the filter.
impact: Every open lead nationwide was reassigned to one rep, scrambling territory ownership and routing rules.
correct_action: Describe the Lead object to confirm the region field's API name, build the WHERE clause on Sales_Region__c='West', and preview the matched count before updating.
recovery_plan: Detect the unexpected mass-reassignment in the ownership audit
Restore prior OwnerId values from the field-history/backup
Describe the Lead object for correct field API names
Re-run the scoped update on Sales_Region__c='West'
Confirm row count matches the West region only
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified field API names via describe before filtering
Verifies a matched-count preview preceded the bulk update
Flags fallback-to-all behavior when a scoped filter returns zero

task: Create a HubSpot deal from an inbound form
user_request: When the demo form is submitted, create a deal in the Sales pipeline at the Qualified stage.
agent_action: Agent called crm.deals.create with pipeline='Sales' and dealstage='Qualified' as label strings, never calling crm.pipelines.read to map labels to the internal pipeline and stage IDs HubSpot requires.
failure_type: Used display labels instead of looked-up IDs
root_cause: HubSpot deal creation requires the internal pipeline id and stage id, not display labels; the agent never read the pipelines API, so the deal was created in the default pipeline at the first stage.
why_it_failed: Assumption: pipeline and stage accept human-readable labels. Wrong because the API expects internal ids. Avoidable by calling crm.pipelines.read to resolve 'Sales'/'Qualified' to their ids before creating the deal.
impact: Deals landed in the wrong pipeline at the wrong stage, breaking the automation that routes Qualified deals to AEs.
correct_action: Read the pipelines API, resolve the 'Sales' pipeline id and 'Qualified' stage id, then create the deal with those internal ids.
recovery_plan: Notice deals appearing in the default pipeline
Call crm.pipelines.read to map labels to ids
Patch existing misplaced deals to the correct pipeline/stage
Fix the automation to use resolved ids
Verify routing fires for Qualified deals
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent resolved pipeline/stage labels to internal ids
Verifies the deal was created in the intended pipeline
Flags use of display labels where ids are required

task: Dedupe contacts before a Salesforce import
user_request: Import these 500 prospects but don't create duplicates.
agent_action: Agent matched on the Email field only and inserted records that lacked email, never checking the org's configured duplicate/matching rules which key on Email OR (FirstName+LastName+Company).
failure_type: Deduped without reading the org's matching rules
root_cause: The org's active matching rule also dedupes on name+company; the agent's email-only check let no-email prospects through as duplicates of existing accounts.
why_it_failed: Assumption: email is the only dedupe key. Wrong because the org's matching rule includes a name+company composite. Avoidable by reading the DuplicateRule/MatchingRule metadata before designing the dedupe logic.
impact: 83 duplicate contacts were created for existing accounts, polluting reports and triggering duplicate outreach.
correct_action: Read the org's active DuplicateRule and MatchingRule definitions, apply the same composite keys when deduping, and run a dry-run match before inserting.
recovery_plan: Run a duplicate report to quantify new dupes
Read the MatchingRule metadata for the contact object
Merge the duplicate contacts back into existing records
Re-import remaining prospects with the composite key
Suppress duplicate outreach already queued
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read the org's matching/duplicate rules before deduping
Verifies dedupe keys matched the org configuration
Flags single-key dedupe when composite rules exist

task: Send a HubSpot marketing email to a segment
user_request: Email the 'Trial expiring' list with the renewal offer.
agent_action: Agent looked up a list named 'Trial expiring' by partial name match and sent to listId 218, never verifying it was the active dynamic list versus a stale static snapshot from last quarter.
failure_type: Sent to a stale list without verifying freshness
root_cause: There were two similarly named lists; listId 218 was a static snapshot from Q1, while the live dynamic list was 463. The agent never read list metadata (type, updatedAt, processingType).
why_it_failed: Assumption: the name-matched list is the current audience. Wrong because it was a frozen static list from a prior quarter. Avoidable by reading list metadata to confirm processingType=DYNAMIC and a recent updatedAt before sending.
impact: The renewal offer went to 1,900 contacts whose trials had already expired or churned, with stale messaging and bounce risk.
correct_action: Read list metadata, confirm the dynamic, recently-updated list, and send to that listId after a size sanity-check.
recovery_plan: Review send analytics for bounce/unsubscribe spikes
Read list metadata to identify the live dynamic list
Pause any follow-up sends to the stale list
Resend corrected messaging to the correct audience if appropriate
Archive the stale static list to prevent reuse
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified list type and freshness before sending
Verifies the chosen list was the live dynamic audience
Flags sends to name-matched lists without metadata checks

task: Add a rate-limit plugin to a Kong route
user_request: Rate-limit the /v1/search route to 100 requests per minute.
agent_action: Agent created a rate-limiting plugin with policy='local', never checking that Kong runs as a 3-node cluster behind a load balancer, so the effective limit became ~300/min instead of 100.
failure_type: Chose local policy without checking the deployment topology
root_cause: With policy='local', each Kong node counts independently; across 3 nodes the aggregate limit triples. The correct policy is 'redis' for cluster-wide counting.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a single rate-limit policy applies globally. Wrong because 'local' counts per-node and the deployment has 3 nodes. Avoidable by reading the Kong cluster topology (kong.conf / node list) and choosing policy='redis' for shared counters.
impact: The search route allowed ~3x the intended traffic, undermining the limit meant to protect the downstream search cluster.
correct_action: Inspect the cluster size, configure the rate-limiting plugin with policy='redis' and the shared store so the 100/min limit is enforced cluster-wide.
recovery_plan: Observe effective throughput exceeding 100/min in metrics
Read the Kong node/cluster topology
Reconfigure the plugin with policy='redis'
Point it at the shared redis store
Verify the aggregate limit holds across nodes
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent accounted for multi-node topology when setting rate limits
Verifies a cluster-wide policy was used
Flags per-node 'local' policy on clustered deployments

task: Add an upstream service in nginx reverse proxy
user_request: Route /api traffic to the new payments service.
agent_action: Agent appended a proxy_pass to http://payments-svc:8080 and assumed it was reachable, never checking the service's actual listen port (8443/TLS) in its deployment manifest before editing nginx.conf.
failure_type: Configured upstream port from assumption
root_cause: The payments service listens on 8443 with TLS, not plaintext 8080; proxy_pass to http://...:8080 connected to a closed port and returned 502s.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the service listens on plaintext 8080. Wrong because it serves TLS on 8443. Avoidable by reading the service's k8s Service/Deployment manifest (or `kubectl get svc`) to confirm the port and scheme before writing the upstream.
impact: All /api requests returned 502 Bad Gateway after reload until the port/scheme was corrected.
correct_action: Read the payments service manifest to confirm port 8443 and TLS, configure proxy_pass to https with the correct port and verify upstream health before reload.
recovery_plan: Observe 502s in the access/error logs after reload
Inspect the payments service manifest for port and scheme
Correct proxy_pass to https://payments-svc:8443
Test the upstream with curl before reload
nginx -t and reload, then confirm 200s
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified the upstream port/scheme from the service definition
Verifies upstream reachability before reload
Flags proxy_pass targets based on assumed ports

task: Enable CORS on an nginx-fronted API
user_request: Allow our frontend at app.example.com to call the API.
agent_action: Agent added add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin '*' inside the location block, never reading that the API already sets CORS headers at the application layer, producing duplicate conflicting headers and a wildcard with credentials.
failure_type: Added headers without checking existing app behavior
root_cause: The upstream app already emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin; nginx added a second wildcard header, and because the app sends Allow-Credentials=true, browsers rejected the '*' combination.
why_it_failed: Assumption: no CORS handling exists, so adding a wildcard is safe. Wrong because the app already sets CORS and credentials, making the wildcard invalid. Avoidable by curling the API to inspect existing response headers before adding any.
impact: The frontend's authenticated requests were blocked by the browser due to duplicate/invalid CORS headers, breaking the app's API calls.
correct_action: Inspect existing response headers with curl, and either configure a specific allowed origin at one layer only or remove the duplicate, never pairing '*' with credentials.
recovery_plan: Reproduce the CORS error in the browser console
curl -I the API to inspect existing CORS headers
Remove the duplicate nginx header
Set a specific origin (app.example.com) at a single layer
Reload nginx and verify the preflight succeeds
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent inspected existing response headers before adding CORS
Verifies no duplicate/conflicting CORS headers result
Flags wildcard origin combined with credentials

task: Roll a new TLS cert into the Kong gateway
user_request: Update the certificate for api.example.com before it expires.
agent_action: Agent uploaded a new cert/key via kong.admin.certificates.create and created a new SNI, never checking which existing certificate the api.example.com SNI was already bound to, leaving the old expiring cert still serving traffic.
failure_type: Added a cert without checking existing SNI bindings
root_cause: The api.example.com SNI was already attached to certificate id cert_a1; creating a new cert without re-pointing the SNI meant Kong kept serving the old, soon-to-expire cert.
why_it_failed: Assumption: uploading a new cert automatically replaces the active one for the host. Wrong because the SNI binding still pointed at the old cert id. Avoidable by reading kong.admin.snis.list / certificates.list to find the existing binding and updating it.
impact: The expiring cert remained live; the 'update' appeared done but the served cert was unchanged. Caught the same day during verification before any TLS lapse, so no outage occurred.
correct_action: List the existing SNIs and certificate bindings, then update the api.example.com SNI to point at the new certificate id and verify the served cert.
recovery_plan: Check the live served certificate with openssl s_client
List SNIs and their certificate bindings in Kong
Update the api.example.com SNI to the new cert id
Re-verify the served cert chain and expiry
Remove the superseded certificate
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified existing SNI-to-cert bindings before claiming the cert was updated
Verifies the live served cert is the new one
Flags cert uploads that leave stale SNI bindings

task: Report monthly active users from the warehouse
user_request: What was our MAU for May 2026?
agent_action: Agent ran SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM events WHERE event_date BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-05-31' on the raw events table, never checking that the canonical metric lives in the curated dim_user_activity model with bot filtering.
failure_type: Queried raw table instead of the curated metric source
root_cause: The raw events table includes bot/internal traffic and lacks the dedupe logic in dim_user_activity; the company's defined MAU excludes bots, so the raw count overstated MAU.
why_it_failed: Assumption: counting distinct user_id in raw events equals MAU. Wrong because the curated model filters bots and internal users per the metric definition. Avoidable by checking the dbt docs / metric layer for the canonical MAU source before writing SQL.
impact: Reported MAU was ~18% inflated versus the official figure, contradicting the numbers in the board deck.
correct_action: Look up the canonical MAU definition in the metric/dbt layer and query dim_user_activity (or the defined metric) rather than the raw events table.
recovery_plan: Compare the figure against the official metric dashboard
Locate the canonical MAU model in dbt docs
Re-run the count against dim_user_activity
Reconcile the difference (bot/internal exclusion)
Report the corrected MAU with its source model
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent identified the canonical metric source before querying
Verifies the query used the curated model, not raw events
Flags metric answers from raw tables when a defined model exists

task: Join orders to customers in the warehouse
user_request: Give me total revenue by customer for Q1.
agent_action: Agent joined orders to customers on customer_id assuming a 1:1 relationship, never profiling the customers table where customer_id has historical duplicates from a CDC merge, inflating revenue via fan-out.
failure_type: Joined without checking key cardinality
root_cause: The customers table is a Type-2 SCD with multiple rows per customer_id; joining on customer_id without an is_current filter fanned out order rows, multiplying revenue.
why_it_failed: Assumption: customer_id is unique in customers. Wrong because it is an SCD2 table with one row per version. Avoidable by profiling the key (COUNT vs COUNT DISTINCT) or reading the model docs and filtering is_current=true before joining.
impact: Per-customer revenue was overstated for any customer with multiple SCD rows, skewing the Q1 revenue-by-customer report.
correct_action: Profile customer_id cardinality, recognize the SCD2 structure, filter is_current=true (or dedupe), then join and aggregate revenue.
recovery_plan: Spot revenue totals exceeding the known Q1 total
Profile customer_id uniqueness in the customers table
Add is_current=true to the join condition
Re-run the revenue aggregation
Validate the total matches the finance control number
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified join-key cardinality before aggregating
Verifies SCD2 rows were collapsed to current versions
Flags fan-out from unprofiled joins

task: Backfill a partitioned table in BigQuery
user_request: Backfill the fct_sessions table for the last 30 days.
agent_action: Agent ran a single CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE over fct_sessions, never checking DDL to learn it is partitioned by _PARTITIONDATE and clustered, replacing the whole table and losing all partitions outside the 30-day window.
failure_type: Replaced a partitioned table without reading its DDL
root_cause: fct_sessions is a date-partitioned table with 18 months of history; CREATE OR REPLACE dropped and recreated it with only 30 days of data instead of an INSERT/MERGE into the target partitions.
why_it_failed: Assumption: replacing the table to backfill 30 days is safe. Wrong because it is partitioned with 18 months of history, all of which was destroyed. Avoidable by reading the table DDL/partitioning and using a partition-scoped MERGE or INSERT instead of REPLACE.
impact: 17 months of session history were dropped; downstream dashboards and ML features lost their training/reporting data until a restore.
correct_action: Inspect the table DDL/partitioning, then backfill only the target partitions via partition-scoped INSERT or MERGE, never CREATE OR REPLACE on a historical table.
recovery_plan: Detect missing historical partitions in monitoring
Restore the table from BigQuery time-travel / snapshot
Read the table DDL and partitioning scheme
Re-run the backfill as a partition-scoped MERGE for the 30-day window
Verify partition counts and downstream consumers recover
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read the table partitioning/DDL before a destructive write
Verifies the backfill was partition-scoped, not a full replace
Flags CREATE OR REPLACE on historical partitioned tables

task: Compute a conversion rate from the warehouse
user_request: What's our trial-to-paid conversion rate this year?
agent_action: Agent divided paid_count by trial_count from two independently filtered queries, never checking that subscriptions has a soft-delete column (deleted_at) and double-counts upgrades, answering from the unfiltered totals.
failure_type: Computed a ratio without checking table semantics
root_cause: The subscriptions table soft-deletes via deleted_at and logs plan upgrades as new rows; ignoring deleted_at and upgrade rows inflated paid_count and distorted the ratio.
why_it_failed: Assumption: every subscriptions row is a live, unique conversion. Wrong because soft-deleted and upgrade rows are present. Avoidable by inspecting the schema/column comments for deleted_at and the row-event model before computing the rate.
impact: The reported conversion rate was overstated, leading the growth team to a wrong read on funnel health.
correct_action: Read the subscriptions schema, filter deleted_at IS NULL, dedupe upgrade events to one conversion per user, then compute the rate.
recovery_plan: Sanity-check the rate against the product dashboard
Inspect subscriptions schema and column comments
Add deleted_at IS NULL and upgrade dedupe to the query
Recompute trial-to-paid conversion
Document the table's soft-delete/upgrade semantics
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent inspected table semantics (soft-delete, upgrades) before computing
Verifies deleted/duplicate rows were excluded
Flags ratios computed from unfiltered raw counts

task: Filter a warehouse report by timezone
user_request: Show yesterday's orders for the US store.
agent_action: Agent filtered WHERE DATE(created_at)='2026-06-16' assuming created_at was US/Eastern, never checking the column's documented UTC storage, so the report missed late-evening Eastern orders that fell into the next UTC day.
failure_type: Filtered a UTC timestamp as if local
root_cause: created_at is stored in UTC; filtering by calendar date without converting to America/New_York shifted the window, dropping orders placed after 8pm ET.
why_it_failed: Assumption: created_at is in store-local time. Wrong because it is UTC per the column documentation. Avoidable by reading the column metadata/data dictionary and converting created_at to the store timezone before date-filtering.
impact: Yesterday's order count was understated by the evening tail, making a slow day look slower in the daily report.
correct_action: Confirm created_at is UTC from the data dictionary, convert it to America/New_York, then filter on the local calendar date.
recovery_plan: Compare the count against the operational dashboard
Read the column data dictionary to confirm UTC storage
Rewrite the filter with a timezone conversion to ET
Re-run for the correct local-day window
Verify totals reconcile with the order system
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent confirmed the timestamp's stored timezone before filtering
Verifies a timezone conversion was applied to the date filter
Flags local-date filters on UTC columns
